transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Could you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brought me in is… I’ve been getting really caught up in this scar on my wrist. I know, logically, it’s probably not nearly as noticeable as it seems to me, and part of me feels silly even saying it out loud. But when I’m around people—like at church, or when I’m playing bridge—I feel like everyone’s eyes go straight to it.

It’s like before I can even settle into a conversation, I’m wondering if they’ve noticed it, or if they’re thinking about it, like it’s the first thing they see about me now. I keep trying to tell myself people have better things to look at or think about, but it still feels so obvious to me. It’s been bothering me enough that I thought maybe I should talk to someone about it.
Does this concern about your scar cause you a lot of distress, or has it affected your ability to do things you normally would, like going to church or playing bridge?

Yes… it has, more than I’d like to admit. I mean, I’m still doing things, mostly, but it slows me down and makes me avoid certain things.

With my bookkeeping work, I’ve been late turning things in because I’ll get caught up before I leave the house or before I sit down to work, trying different sleeves or bracelets or positioning my wrist so it won’t show. And then I lose time, and I’m already worked up, so it takes me longer to focus.

And socially… yes, I’ve skipped some choir things at church and a couple of volunteer commitments with the theater group because I just couldn’t get past the idea that people would notice my wrist. It sounds so small when I say it, but in the moment it feels like I have to fix it or hide it before I can even show up.
Do you find yourself thinking about the scar for a significant amount of time each day, maybe more than an hour, or does it feel hard to control those thoughts?

Yes… it does feel hard to control, especially once I’m somewhere with other people. I don’t know if I’m counting the minutes exactly, but it can take over my mind in a way that feels bigger than it should.

Like at church, I’ll be sitting there trying to listen, and then I’ll suddenly think, “Can they see my wrist from this angle?” or “Did that person look down at it?” And then I’m not really present anymore. Same with bridge — I’ll be trying to focus on the cards, but I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to the scar, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.

And I do know, somewhere in my head, that it probably isn’t as bad as it looks to me. I know people may not even be paying attention. But that doesn’t stop the feeling. Once the thought is there, it just sort of keeps circling.

When you’re worried about the scar being noticeable, do you find yourself doing certain things over and over—like checking how it looks, covering it, or asking others if it’s okay—to try to feel more reassured?

Yes… I do. I wish I didn’t, because I can see how it probably sounds a little excessive, but before I leave the house I’ll check my wrist in the hall mirror, usually more than once. I’ll look at it one way, then turn my arm, then think maybe the light is making it look worse, so I’ll check it again from another angle.

And then I’ll start fussing with what I’m wearing. I’ll try a blouse with longer sleeves, or I’ll put on a bracelet and see if it distracts from it or covers it enough. Sometimes I change back and forth a few times, which is embarrassing to admit, because it’s just my wrist, but it feels very hard to leave it alone once I’ve noticed it.

I do ask my husband sometimes, too. I’ll say, “Does this look obvious?” or “Can you see it right away?” And he always tells me it’s barely there, that nobody would notice it. I believe that he’s trying to be kind, and maybe he’s right, but it only settles me for a little while. Then I’ll start wondering if he’s just saying that because he’s my husband.

When you think about the scar, do you ever feel like it’s not just noticeable but somehow worse than others seem to realize—like there’s something about it that others don’t understand or aren’t seeing the way you do?

Yes… I think that’s a good way to put it. I don’t think I’d say I’m convinced everyone is lying to me or anything like that, because part of me does know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. I can sort of understand that, logically.

But when I’m actually out somewhere, like at church or when I’m playing bridge, it feels different. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly I’m sure people’s eyes are going right to my wrist, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now. And then I think, well, maybe they’re just being polite and not saying anything, or maybe they don’t realize how obvious it is because they’re not looking at it the way I am.

So… yes, I suppose I do feel like there’s something about it that I’m seeing more clearly than other people are, even though another part of me knows I may be making it larger in my mind than it really is. It’s confusing, because I don’t want to be vain or dramatic about it, but in the moment it feels very real.

When you're focused on the scar, is it mainly the idea that it looks physically unattractive or flawed in a way that others don't seem to see, or is it more about intrusive, upsetting thoughts that keep coming back regardless of how it looks?

I think it’s more about how it looks… how it looks to me, anyway. It’s not just a random thought that pops in and bothers me no matter what. It’s really tied to the scar being there on my wrist and feeling like it looks unattractive, or obvious, or like there’s something flawed about it that other people either don’t notice or don’t admit they notice.

I do know, in a more reasonable part of my mind, that it’s probably not as bad as it seems to me. I can say that sitting here. But when I’m at church, or when I’m playing bridge, it doesn’t feel small at all. I’ll be trying to listen or pay attention to the game, and I keep having this feeling that everyone’s eyes go straight to my wrist, like it’s the first thing they see about me now. And then I feel so self-conscious, like I want to turn my arm or hide it without making it obvious that I’m hiding it.

So yes, I’d say it’s mainly about the appearance of it — the idea that it looks flawed or noticeable in a way that maybe other people don’t see the same way I do.
Do you find yourself worrying about other parts of your body in the same way you worry about your wrist scar, or is this concern mainly limited to the scar itself?

It’s mainly the scar itself. I mean, I can have the usual complaints anyone has at my age, I suppose, but nothing that takes hold of me the way this does.

With the wrist, it’s like once I notice it, I can’t quite un-notice it. I know, sitting here, that it’s probably not as bad as it looks to me. I do know that. But when I’m at church, or sitting at bridge, I start feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it — like it’s the first thing they notice about me now. And then I get caught up in thinking about how my arm is positioned, whether the light is hitting it, whether I should turn my wrist a little.

So no, it’s not really other parts of my body in the same way. It’s this scar. It’s small, probably, to other people, but to me it starts feeling very obvious.

When you're worried about people noticing your scar, is your main concern that they will judge you negatively as a person because of it, or is your main concern that the scar itself looks worse than others seem to realize?

I think it’s more the second one… that the scar itself looks worse than other people seem to realize. I don’t exactly think they’re judging my whole character or thinking I’m a bad person because of it. It’s not quite that.

It’s more that I feel like they must be seeing this mark on my wrist, and maybe they’re just being kind or polite by not saying anything. I know, sitting here talking to you, that it’s probably not as bad as it looks to me. I can say that. But when I’m at church, or when I’m at bridge and my hand is out on the table, it just feels like everyone’s eyes go straight to it, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.

And then I start thinking, maybe they don’t understand how obvious it is, or maybe they’re seeing it but pretending not to. So no, I wouldn’t say my main fear is that they’ll judge me as a person. It’s more that the scar feels so noticeable and unattractive to me, and I can’t quite believe other people don’t see it that way too.
Has this concern about your wrist scar ever led to problems in your relationships, work, or other important areas of your life that we haven't talked about yet?

Yes… it has, though I feel a little embarrassed saying that because it sounds so small when I put it into words. But it has interfered.

With my bookkeeping work, there have been times I’ve been late turning things in because I get stuck before I leave the house, trying to decide what to wear or how to position my sleeve so my wrist won’t show. Or I’ll sit down to work and I’m supposed to be concentrating on figures, and instead I’m looking at my wrist or thinking about whether someone noticed it earlier, and then I lose time. It’s not that I can’t do the work, exactly, but I’ve turned things in later than I should have because I got caught up in all of that.

And I’ve skipped some things too. I sing in the choir, and I help with theater volunteer work sometimes, and there have been days where I just… didn’t go. I told myself I was tired or that they had enough people, but really it was because I kept imagining standing there under lights or sitting where people could see my arm, and I couldn’t stop thinking about whether the scar would be noticeable.

So yes, it’s not ruining everything, but it has caused problems. More than I’d like to admit.
When you think about the scar, are you ever worried that it might be a sign of something more serious, like a disease or a deeper health problem?

No, I don’t think that’s really where my mind goes. I’m not sitting there thinking it’s a disease, exactly, or that it means something is wrong inside me. It’s more… I don’t like the way it looks, and I get stuck on that.

I suppose if I’m being very precise, I worry about what it looks like on the surface — the color of it, the way the skin catches the light, whether it seems raised or obvious. But I’m not usually thinking, “Oh, this is cancer,” or “this means I’m ill.” It isn’t that kind of fear.

It’s more vain than that, I guess, though I hate saying it that way. It just feels ugly to me, and then I can’t stop noticing it.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or changing your behavior specifically because of how the scar looks, beyond just trying to cover it up?

Yes… yes, I do. It’s not only covering it, though that’s part of it. It’s more that I start arranging whole little pieces of my day around whether my wrist might be seen, and then it gets away from me.

Like with my bookkeeping work, I’ve been late turning things in because I get caught up before I even leave the house, fussing with what I’m wearing or thinking through whether I’ll have to reach across a desk or hand someone papers. And then sometimes I lose time just trying to make sure my wrist won’t be noticed, or I get so preoccupied with it that I’m not focusing the way I should.

And I’ve skipped things I actually care about, too. Choir, for example, and some of the theater volunteer commitments. I’ll tell myself, “Oh, they have enough people,” or “I’m too tired tonight,” but if I’m honest, a lot of it is that I imagine being there and someone seeing my wrist, especially if my arm is out or there are lights or people close by. Then I talk myself out of going.

So yes, I guess I do change my behavior. I don’t like admitting that, because it sounds excessive, but I have avoided things because of how the scar looks.
Do you ever spend a lot of time grooming or adjusting your appearance in front of mirrors or other reflective surfaces because of the way the scar looks?

Yes… I do. More than I’d like to admit, honestly.

Before I leave the house, especially if I’m going somewhere where I’ll be around people, I’ll stop at the hall mirror and check my wrist. Not just once, usually. I’ll look, then step away, then come back and look again, because I’ll think maybe the light was different or maybe I didn’t really see how noticeable it was. I’ll turn my arm a little, pull my sleeve down, push it back up to see if it slips, that sort of thing.

Sometimes I’ll change sleeves more than once — like I’ll think one blouse covers it, but then if I reach for something, the cuff moves and I can see it, so then I try another top. Or I’ll put on a bracelet and fuss with where it sits, whether it covers the scar or draws more attention to it. It can get a bit ridiculous, standing there adjusting something so small.

And I do ask my husband sometimes, “Does this look obvious?” or “Can you see it?” He always says it’s barely there, and I know he means to reassure me, but I don’t always believe it. Or I believe him for maybe a minute, and then I look again anyway.

When you're worried about the scar being noticeable, do you feel a strong need to perform certain behaviors, like checking your wrist repeatedly or adjusting your clothes in a specific way, because you believe something bad will happen if you don't?

I don’t know that I think something terrible will happen exactly, not in a superstitious way, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I think, “If I don’t check it three times, something bad will happen.” But I do feel very uncomfortable if I haven’t checked it, like I can’t quite settle or leave the house without making sure.

Usually before I go out, I’ll stop in the hall mirror and look at my wrist a few times. I’ll turn it different ways, because sometimes it looks worse depending on the light or the angle. Then I’ll fuss with my sleeve — pull it down, see if it stays, reach my arm out a little to test whether it rides up. Sometimes I’ll change tops if I think the sleeve isn’t covering it right.

And then there’s the bracelet thing. I’ll try one and then wonder if it covers the scar or if it actually makes people look at my wrist more, so I’ll switch it or take it off or put it back on. It can take longer than it should.

I do ask my husband too, “Can you see it?” or “Does this look obvious?” And he always says it’s barely there, that no one would notice, but I still feel like I need to hear it. It calms me down for a little while, even if I don’t fully believe it. So yes, I suppose there is a need to do those things, but it’s more to feel reassured than because I think something awful will happen if I don’t.
Do you feel anxious or distressed when you’re not able to check your wrist or adjust your clothing in the way you’d like?

Yes… I do get anxious, or at least very unsettled, if I can’t do it the way I want to.

It’s usually before I leave the house. I have this little routine now, I suppose — I stop at the hall mirror and check my wrist a few times, not just once. I’ll turn it one way and then another, because if the light catches it differently I feel like it looks more obvious. And if I’m rushed or someone is waiting for me and I can’t really look properly, I feel this kind of nagging discomfort, like I’m leaving without knowing whether it’s showing.

The clothing part is the same. If the sleeve doesn’t sit right, I’ll keep pulling it down or trying to see if it will cover the scar when I move my arm. Sometimes I’ll try a different top altogether. Or I’ll put on a bracelet and then fuss over whether it hides it or actually draws attention to it, which is silly, but I can’t seem to let it go quickly.

And if I can’t ask my husband, “Does it look obvious?” I feel less reassured. He always says it’s barely there, and part of me knows he’s probably right, but hearing it helps me calm down for a bit. So yes, when I can’t check or adjust, I feel tense and distracted, like I haven’t finished something I need to finish before I can go out.

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me, but when I’m at church or bridge I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the focus is on the scar being physically unattractive or flawed in a way others do not see, which directly matches appearance-related preoccupation with a perceived defect.

patient.answer:
I think it’s more about how it looks… how it looks to me, anyway. It’s not just a random thought that pops in and bothers me no matter what. It’s really tied to the scar being there on my wrist and feeling like it looks unattractive, or obvious, or like there’s something flawed about it that other people either don’t notice or don’t admit they notice.

I do know, in a more reasonable part of my mind, that it’s probably not as bad as it seems to me. I can say that sitting here. But when I’m at church, or when I’m playing bridge, it doesn’t feel small at all. I’ll be trying to listen or pay attention to the game, and I keep having this feeling that everyone’s eyes go straight to my wrist, like it’s the first thing they see about me now. And then I feel so self-conscious, like I want to turn my arm or hide it without making it obvious that I’m hiding it.

So yes, I’d say it’s mainly about the appearance of it — the idea that it looks flawed or noticeable in a way that maybe other people don’t see the same way I do.

inference.note: The patient's concerns are primarily focused on the perceived physical appearance of a scar, causing significant distress and avoidance behaviors. This aligns more with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.2), which was not previously considered. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42.8) remains plausible due to intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors, but the primary focus on appearance makes F45.2 more likely. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22) were ruled out due to the specific focus on a physical feature.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern about the scar is part of a broader pattern of appearance-related preoccupations that could suggest body dysmorphic disorder (F42.8) rather than obsessive-compulsive disorder (F45.2), by asking if they have similar concerns about other body parts.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying about other parts of your body in the same way you worry about your wrist scar, or is this concern mainly limited to the scar itself?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the scope of the appearance preoccupation—whether it involves other perceived body flaws or is mainly limited to the wrist scar.

patient.answer:
It’s mainly the scar itself. I mean, I can have the usual complaints anyone has at my age, I suppose, but nothing that takes hold of me the way this does.

With the wrist, it’s like once I notice it, I can’t quite un-notice it. I know, sitting here, that it’s probably not as bad as it looks to me. I do know that. But when I’m at church, or sitting at bridge, I start feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it — like it’s the first thing they notice about me now. And then I get caught up in thinking about how my arm is positioned, whether the light is hitting it, whether I should turn my wrist a little.

So no, it’s not really other parts of my body in the same way. It’s this scar. It’s small, probably, to other people, but to me it starts feeling very obvious.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern about the scar is better explained by a preoccupation with perceived physical defect (as in body dysmorphic disorder) or by anxiety about being judged by others (as in social anxiety disorder).
doctor.question: When you're worried about people noticing your scar, is your main concern that they will judge you negatively as a person because of it, or is your main concern that the scar itself looks worse than others seem to realize?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me, but when I’m at church or bridge I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the concern is mainly about the scar itself looking flawed or worse than others perceive, which directly matches preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect.

patient.answer:
I think it’s more the second one… that the scar itself looks worse than other people seem to realize. I don’t exactly think they’re judging my whole character or thinking I’m a bad person because of it. It’s not quite that.

It’s more that I feel like they must be seeing this mark on my wrist, and maybe they’re just being kind or polite by not saying anything. I know, sitting here talking to you, that it’s probably not as bad as it looks to me. I can say that. But when I’m at church, or when I’m at bridge and my hand is out on the table, it just feels like everyone’s eyes go straight to it, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.

And then I start thinking, maybe they don’t understand how obvious it is, or maybe they’re seeing it but pretending not to. So no, I wouldn’t say my main fear is that they’ll judge me as a person. It’s more that the scar feels so noticeable and unattractive to me, and I can’t quite believe other people don’t see it that way too.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in daily functioning specifically due to preoccupation with the scar, beyond what has already been described.
doctor.question: Has this concern about your wrist scar ever led to problems in your relationships, work, or other important areas of your life that we haven't talked about yet?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been late turning in bookkeeping work and have skipped some choir and theater volunteer commitments because I get so caught up trying to make sure my wrist won’t be noticed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the wrist scar concern has caused problems in relationships, work, or other important life areas, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… it has, though I feel a little embarrassed saying that because it sounds so small when I put it into words. But it has interfered.

With my bookkeeping work, there have been times I’ve been late turning things in because I get stuck before I leave the house, trying to decide what to wear or how to position my sleeve so my wrist won’t show. Or I’ll sit down to work and I’m supposed to be concentrating on figures, and instead I’m looking at my wrist or thinking about whether someone noticed it earlier, and then I lose time. It’s not that I can’t do the work, exactly, but I’ve turned things in later than I should have because I got caught up in all of that.

And I’ve skipped some things too. I sing in the choir, and I help with theater volunteer work sometimes, and there have been days where I just… didn’t go. I told myself I was tired or that they had enough people, but really it was because I kept imagining standing there under lights or sitting where people could see my arm, and I couldn’t stop thinking about whether the scar would be noticeable.

So yes, it’s not ruining everything, but it has caused problems. More than I’d like to admit.

inference.note: The patient's concern is primarily focused on the appearance of the scar, with significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning. The distinction between Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22) and Other Specified Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorder (F42.8) remains due to overlapping features, but F45.22 is strengthened as the concern is appearance-based rather than purely intrusive thoughts.

doctor.question: When you think about the scar, are you ever worried that it might be a sign of something more serious, like a disease or a deeper health problem?

target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the scar causes worries about disease or a deeper health problem, which is not covered by the listed symptom profiles focused on appearance preoccupation, repetitive appearance-related behaviors, or functional impairment.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think that’s really where my mind goes. I’m not sitting there thinking it’s a disease, exactly, or that it means something is wrong inside me. It’s more… I don’t like the way it looks, and I get stuck on that.

I suppose if I’m being very precise, I worry about what it looks like on the surface — the color of it, the way the skin catches the light, whether it seems raised or obvious. But I’m not usually thinking, “Oh, this is cancer,” or “this means I’m ill.” It isn’t that kind of fear.

It’s more vain than that, I guess, though I hate saying it that way. It just feels ugly to me, and then I can’t stop noticing it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern about the scar is associated with repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to anxiety about appearance, which would support a diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder (F42.8).
doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or changing your behavior specifically because of how the scar looks, beyond just trying to cover it up?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been late turning in bookkeeping work and have skipped some choir and theater volunteer commitments because I get so caught up trying to make sure my wrist won’t be noticed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the appearance concern leads to avoidance or behavior changes that interfere with life, which matches skipping commitments and other functional impairment due to worries about the wrist scar.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I do. It’s not only covering it, though that’s part of it. It’s more that I start arranging whole little pieces of my day around whether my wrist might be seen, and then it gets away from me.

Like with my bookkeeping work, I’ve been late turning things in because I get caught up before I even leave the house, fussing with what I’m wearing or thinking through whether I’ll have to reach across a desk or hand someone papers. And then sometimes I lose time just trying to make sure my wrist won’t be noticed, or I get so preoccupied with it that I’m not focusing the way I should.

And I’ve skipped things I actually care about, too. Choir, for example, and some of the theater volunteer commitments. I’ll tell myself, “Oh, they have enough people,” or “I’m too tired tonight,” but if I’m honest, a lot of it is that I imagine being there and someone seeing my wrist, especially if my arm is out or there are lights or people close by. Then I talk myself out of going.

So yes, I guess I do change my behavior. I don’t like admitting that, because it sounds excessive, but I have avoided things because of how the scar looks.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern about the scar is associated with excessive grooming or appearance-related behaviors beyond covering the scar, which could indicate body dysmorphic disorder (F42.8).
doctor.question: Do you ever spend a lot of time grooming or adjusting your appearance in front of mirrors or other reflective surfaces because of the way the scar looks?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: Before I leave the house, I’ll check my wrist in the hall mirror a few times, try different sleeves or a bracelet to cover it, and sometimes ask my husband if it looks obvious, even though he always says it’s barely there.
target_item.reason: The question is specifically asking about time spent grooming or adjusting appearance in mirrors because of the scar, which matches repetitive appearance-related checking and adjusting behaviors.

patient.answer:
Yes… I do. More than I’d like to admit, honestly.

Before I leave the house, especially if I’m going somewhere where I’ll be around people, I’ll stop at the hall mirror and check my wrist. Not just once, usually. I’ll look, then step away, then come back and look again, because I’ll think maybe the light was different or maybe I didn’t really see how noticeable it was. I’ll turn my arm a little, pull my sleeve down, push it back up to see if it slips, that sort of thing.

Sometimes I’ll change sleeves more than once — like I’ll think one blouse covers it, but then if I reach for something, the cuff moves and I can see it, so then I try another top. Or I’ll put on a bracelet and fuss with where it sits, whether it covers the scar or draws more attention to it. It can get a bit ridiculous, standing there adjusting something so small.

And I do ask my husband sometimes, “Does this look obvious?” or “Can you see it?” He always says it’s barely there, and I know he means to reassure me, but I don’t always believe it. Or I believe him for maybe a minute, and then I look again anyway.

inference.note: The patient's concerns remain focused on the appearance of the scar and behaviors aimed at concealing or checking it, consistent with body dysmorphic disorder (F45.22). However, the presence of intrusive, repetitive thoughts and ritualistic behaviors (e.g., checking the mirror, adjusting clothing repeatedly, seeking reassurance) also support obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.8). No further information has ruled out either diagnosis definitively.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern about the scar is accompanied by a repetitive behavior or mental act that is aimed at reducing anxiety or preventing a dreaded event, which would support a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.8).
doctor.question: When you're worried about the scar being noticeable, do you feel a strong need to perform certain behaviors, like checking your wrist repeatedly or adjusting your clothes in a specific way, because you believe something bad will happen if you don't?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: Before I leave the house, I’ll check my wrist in the hall mirror a few times, try different sleeves or a bracelet to cover it, and sometimes ask my husband if it looks obvious, even though he always says it’s barely there.
target_item.reason: The question asks about repeated checking or adjusting clothes in response to worries about the scar being noticeable, which directly matches appearance-related repetitive behaviors.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I think something terrible will happen exactly, not in a superstitious way, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I think, “If I don’t check it three times, something bad will happen.” But I do feel very uncomfortable if I haven’t checked it, like I can’t quite settle or leave the house without making sure.

Usually before I go out, I’ll stop in the hall mirror and look at my wrist a few times. I’ll turn it different ways, because sometimes it looks worse depending on the light or the angle. Then I’ll fuss with my sleeve — pull it down, see if it stays, reach my arm out a little to test whether it rides up. Sometimes I’ll change tops if I think the sleeve isn’t covering it right.

And then there’s the bracelet thing. I’ll try one and then wonder if it covers the scar or if it actually makes people look at my wrist more, so I’ll switch it or take it off or put it back on. It can take longer than it should.

I do ask my husband too, “Can you see it?” or “Does this look obvious?” And he always says it’s barely there, that no one would notice, but I still feel like I need to hear it. It calms me down for a little while, even if I don’t fully believe it. So yes, I suppose there is a need to do those things, but it’s more to feel reassured than because I think something awful will happen if I don’t.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress specifically when not engaging in the behaviors related to the scar, which would support a diagnosis of OCD rather than BDD.
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or distressed when you’re not able to check your wrist or adjust your clothing in the way you’d like?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: Before I leave the house, I’ll check my wrist in the hall mirror a few times, try different sleeves or a bracelet to cover it, and sometimes ask my husband if it looks obvious, even though he always says it’s barely there.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about distress when unable to perform appearance-related repetitive behaviors such as checking the wrist or adjusting clothing.

patient.answer:
Yes… I do get anxious, or at least very unsettled, if I can’t do it the way I want to.

It’s usually before I leave the house. I have this little routine now, I suppose — I stop at the hall mirror and check my wrist a few times, not just once. I’ll turn it one way and then another, because if the light catches it differently I feel like it looks more obvious. And if I’m rushed or someone is waiting for me and I can’t really look properly, I feel this kind of nagging discomfort, like I’m leaving without knowing whether it’s showing.

The clothing part is the same. If the sleeve doesn’t sit right, I’ll keep pulling it down or trying to see if it will cover the scar when I move my arm. Sometimes I’ll try a different top altogether. Or I’ll put on a bracelet and then fuss over whether it hides it or actually draws attention to it, which is silly, but I can’t seem to let it go quickly.

And if I can’t ask my husband, “Does it look obvious?” I feel less reassured. He always says it’s barely there, and part of me knows he’s probably right, but hearing it helps me calm down for a bit. So yes, when I can’t check or adjust, I feel tense and distracted, like I haven’t finished something I need to finish before I can go out.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms are primarily focused on a preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (the wrist scar), leading to repetitive behaviors (checking, covering, reassurance seeking) and significant distress/impairment. There is no evidence of delusional beliefs about the appearance, which rules out F42.8 (Other specified mental disorders). The clinical picture aligns with Body Dysmorphic Disorder, which is coded under F45.22.
